overview.text: Red is a family of hues perceived when light stimulates vision in a way associated with the long-wavelength edge of the visible spectrum; NASA places that edge near 700 nanometers, beyond which lies invisible infrared. It is not one single wavelength or one fixed pigment: hue varies continuously, and red paints and dyes can be made from different materials. Red’s role as a “primary” depends on the mixing system: it is primary for combining emitted light (RGB), but printing inks use cyan, magenta, and yellow. Its meanings also depend on culture; for example, Smithsonian’s National Museum of Asian Art describes red in China as linked with celebration, prosperity, power, and good fortune.

key_facts.text: NASA gives the typical visible-light range as about 380–700 nanometers; red is near its long-wavelength edge, and infrared is beyond what people can see.
On screens and in other additive-light systems, red is one of the red-green-blue primaries; red plus green light appears yellow.
In subtractive color mixing used for printing, cyan, magenta, and yellow are the primaries; combining magenta and yellow can produce red.
Red is not one fixed material: the museum describes vermilion as a red pigment made from cinnabar or produced synthetically, and notes that artworks use varied red pigments and dyes.

In the Chinese contexts described by the National Museum of Asian Art, red has been associated with celebration, prosperity, power, and good fortune; these are cultural meanings, not universal definitions.
